object_types.name: Incident
object_types.definition: An event declared/tracked in the incident management system, representing something breaking that needs investigation and resolution.

source_references.excerpt: Something breaks. We find out about it, one way or another. Somebody declares an incident, somebody runs it, we fix it, we write it up.
Incident number. INC-, then a sequence.

object_types.name: Alert
object_types.definition: A notification of a potential problem, either automatically fired by the monitoring platform or manually raised by an engineer.

source_references.excerpt: Monitoring fires an alert, or a customer tells us.
Alert ID. Comes from the monitoring platform.
If an engineer spots something, they raise it, and raising it creates an alert record. It's a manual alert but it's still an alert.

object_types.name: Ticket
object_types.definition: A customer support ticket reporting an issue, from a separate system than alerts/incidents.

source_references.excerpt: Or a customer tells us and monitoring never fires, which is the embarrassing one.
And a ticket has a ticket number. Different system, different format, always has.

object_types.name: Severity
object_types.definition: The technical impact / blast radius classification of an incident, from SEV1 (severe) to SEV4 (minor).

source_references.excerpt: SEV1 through SEV4. It's about blast radius and technical impact.

object_types.name: Priority
object_types.definition: The customer-urgency classification of an incident, from P1 to P4, independent of severity.

source_references.excerpt: And priority is P1 through P4.

object_types.name: Incident State
object_types.definition: The lifecycle state of an incident.

source_references.excerpt: Triage, declared, mitigated, resolved, closed.

object_types.name: Person
object_types.definition: An individual who can serve as an incident commander (a role, not a job title).

source_references.excerpt: The incident commander. One person, named, and it's a role for the duration, not a job title.

object_types.name: Team
object_types.definition: A group that owns a service on a standing basis.

source_references.excerpt: A team. Services are owned by teams. People move.

object_types.name: Service
object_types.definition: A system/service that can be affected by incidents and is owned by exactly one team.

ambiguities.description: Nadia and the facilitator initially disagree about whether an incident can originate 'from nowhere in particular' (e.g., an engineer noticing something by eye). This is resolved in-transcript (a manual alert is still an alert), but shows an early ambiguity in the origin rule before correction.

source_references.excerpt: Someone noticing something by eye? It happens... No, actually, let me correct that. If an engineer spots something, they raise it, and raising it creates an alert record.

ambiguities.description: Whether severity/priority changes over time should be modeled as attributes of the Incident record (current value only) or as a full history/timeline entity is left ambiguous -- the facilitator explicitly decides to model only the current value and 'note' that history exists in a separate timeline concept that is not otherwise specified or modeled.

source_references.excerpt: Constantly. Severity gets revised as we understand the blast radius... In the timeline, as events. The incident record carries the current severity. ... I'll model the current one and note that changes exist in the timeline.

ambiguities.description: The status 'monitoring' (between mitigated and resolved) is used informally by people (Owen) but is explicitly rejected as a real state by Nadia and the facilitator since it's not in the system dropdown. This is a genuine terminology/process disagreement about whether the five official states fully capture practice.

source_references.excerpt: There's also "monitoring," which sits between mitigated and resolved... That's not a state, that's a thing people write in the channel... If it's not in the system I'm not modelling it. Five states.

ambiguities.description: The term 'owner' is explicitly flagged as ambiguous/overloaded in practice, referring either to the Incident Commander (a temporary role for an incident) or the Service Owner (a standing team assignment) -- both are modeled as distinct fact types but the transcript notes real-world confusion between the two.

source_references.excerpt: Is there a different sense of owner? ... The service owner is the team that owns the broken thing... in a channel, "who owns this?" means either. It's genuinely ambiguous every single time.

ambiguities.description: 'Severity' and 'priority' are colloquially conflated by staff who say 'sev' to mean either concept, despite being formally independent and uncorrelated (explicitly disproven by counterexamples). This is a stated real-world terminology collision, not a modeling decision, but worth flagging as a source of requirement confusion.

source_references.excerpt: And people say "sev" when they mean either... A P1 is always a SEV1. ... That is not true... Halberd Financial goes down... That's a P1 all day. It's a SEV3.

ambiguities.description: Whether the duplicate-of ring's acyclic/no-chain rule is an enforced database constraint or merely an intended business rule is explicitly left unresolved -- Kit states it 'should' hold and is 'the rule as intended' but 'it's not enforced' and chains up to two-deep have been observed in practice.

source_references.excerpt: But nothing stops you making a chain and I've seen two-deep ones... That's the rule as intended. It's not enforced.

ambiguities.description: The final and central unresolved issue: whether incidents later found to be caused by customer misconfiguration should be reclassified, excluded from reliability metrics, or left as-is is explicitly undecided and escalated to Ravi. No 'cause classification' concept exists in the current model, and the facilitator explicitly states this gap is deliberate, not an oversight -- a clear edge case flagged at the end of the transcript.

source_references.excerpt: Is there a decision here today? ... Whether an incident later found to be caused by customer misconfiguration should be reclassified, excluded from reliability metrics, or left as-is, is undecided. The model today captures the five states and does not include any concept of a cause classification, because there isn't one to capture.

ambiguities.description: The facilitator initially misstates the commander rule as universal ('Every incident has exactly one commander'), which Nadia corrects to apply only to declared incidents -- this mirrors an earlier near-mistake by Nadia herself (line 109), suggesting this is a recurring, easy-to-get-wrong nuance in the domain that could trip up future modeling or reporting.

source_references.excerpt: Every incident has exactly one commander. ... No. ... Every _declared_ incident has a commander. Triage incidents have none... Declared incidents have exactly one commander; triage incidents have none.
